Really at the end of the day the current US system is better for the rich while the UK's NHS is better for the poor. Having to wait an extra few months or whatever for something that isn't immediately life threatening is preferable to being stuck with a 5-figure bill at least for the poor and even the lower middle class.

More choice is always better, but I would always argue that government choices end up being less efficient and therefore more costly. Like I said earlier, if you do not have a critical issue the UK system is fine. Get unusual or time sensitive and then we start to see the breakdown. Also sucks to be old with that system. But even with that system you could automate all the mundane and typical and cut out the hard to train and expensive primary healthcare contacts, but that would be even less likely with a system that allows change at the speed of government.

Price transparency, strip ama of power (allow more doctors to be created), loosen FDA restrictions (allow neighbor joe to run an ultrasound for 1/100 the cost of having a tech at a hospital do it), fix the prescription system (if i am on something for the rest of my life, don't require that i make a $100 doctor's visit every year), allow pharmacies to do basic lab work for self dianoses, etc.

Trump mentioned some of these, but we'll see what happens. Rand's bill looked very promising, but by the time the GOPe and DEMe get through it...
For drugs I say end the war on drugs and let anything be bought over the counter to bring down prices. Also create an NHS which gives them to those who need them for nothing.

even as prescriptions they could be super cheap, the problem is that the FDA is granting sole distribution for some medications, even for generics; and many drugs that aren't generics should be, but through some loophole are not.
I'm also opposed to the patent system. All patents but medicine patents especially. Just let anyone make and sell anything with no monopolies.

A UK-style NHS ideally. That system seems to make more efficient use of money as well as provide better quality care. At the very least I'd like a "medicare by default" systen where people without insurance will pay an extra tax if they have income.

I'd like to see something similar to Switzerland except the basic tier being single payer. The cliff notes there:

  • there is a publicly regulated bare minimum standard all insurance providers must offer. this tier is purely not-for profit - 100% of revenue from this plan must go right back to payers.

  • all citizens are required to purchase this tier. it can cost no more than 8% of an individual's personal income. if it would be more than 8% of an individual's personal income than that excess is subsidized.

  • companies can offer additional tiers for profit. for instance if you're not satisfied with the frequency of allowed dental visits in the basic tier, you could buy a more expanded plan.

I'd like to see single payer for a variety of reasons. A big one is simplicity. There would be no need for enforcement clauses on the insurance mandate - no fines for instance. There would also be a greatly reduced administrative expense at the government level as well as the medical level. And of course there'd be no ACA style disaster where everybody is racing to signup and trying to figure out what's going on. You're a citizen? You're enrolled. Simple.

The huge downside with single payer is the potential for corruption. Politicians who received "donations" from various interested parties might voluntarily opt into unreasonable deals which the taxpayer would then shoulder. Developing a new jet fighter shouldn't cost $1.5 trillion. But when our politicians directly negotiate with companies, that's what we the taxpayer end up paying. Of course it also goes the other way. If our representatives were actually there to do the best for the country, single payer ought be able to achieve the lowest possible prices for the nation.

Whatever the new one is, it would be nice to have health insurance that works based on risk. Healthy individuals that exercise regularly, maintain a healthy weight, and generally only go to the doctor for their annual check up and the occasional cold/flu prescription should pay the LEAST. People living unhealthy lifestyles should pay more since they are probably using it more (more claims).

First thing to do is get employers the hell out of it. Employer sponsored health care is a relic of a failed WWII socialist wage cap and now causes all sorts of trouble, from the Hobby Lobby nonsense to age discrimination laws. This reform needs to happen regardless of whatever other reforms are up for consideration.

The more complicated part is the pre-existing conditions thing. Pre-Obamacare, sick people could become uninsurable if their insurer declined to renew a policy that would be lose them money every month. Post-Obamacare, healthy people are forced to buy a policy that is way overpriced relative to their actuarial risk profile. Both those things are bad and I think there is a free market option. Encourage insurers to write policies where, if their insured is diagnosed with a chronic illness and later drops their insurance, the insurer must pay the expected lifetime cost of treatment for that diagnosis (either to another insurance company willing to assume the patient's risk or to the patient while they are uninsured). Healthy people would still pay higher rates, but they would get something of value for the extra cost, namely insurance against premium hikes if they get sick.)
